readability.summary: The workspaces are documented where they are defined and at each place they pass through. The registry's module says what a workspace is on a device, why its record and its replica are written in one transaction, where an ID comes from, why roots are compared by the identity of their directories, and that opening and closing set a client's foreground and nothing else; the crate root names its one module and the slots that later tasks fill. The protocol says which version has the workspace messages, that a window names no client and binds no agent, and what each refusal means; the host's documentation says under which client it keeps the foreground, where a new ID comes from, how a list is paged and what it does when its store fails; the window's backend says what becomes of a request that does not fit one message. The new TypeScript module opens with how the window's folder and its client's foreground workspace are kept one, what Theia keeps and what Nexees keeps, and that every window is still one client. Tests name the behaviour they prove. Review against the final code renamed the window's identifier check, which was named for views and now checks workspace IDs too, with the tooling test that holds its bound to the shared core's, and the helper that accepts an identifier or none, which was named for the foreground; made the switcher's header say that the tree is the foreground workspace's once the host has answered, rather than always, and name the one exception, a folder that cannot be a workspace, which the README now names too; made the protocol's note on a workspace entry say that a window names a workspace by its ID or its root; documented the host's function that creates a workspace; and made the domain's note on path aliases, which named this task for checks of paths that it does not write, name the workspace scope and import instead. During the implementation the window's checks of a name and a root were made to refuse every control character the host refuses, C1 included, so that the window never sends what the host would answer by closing the channel; a window's claims of its folder were made to run one after the other, so that two cannot both create its workspace; and the end-to-end test's waits for the page's DevTools were bounded after a run hung, most likely on a question the page did not answer. The recheck before the commit read the evidence record again, claim by claim against the code, the logs and the session's record, and mended six statements of it (TASK-013_EVIDENCE.md sections 8 to 11).

cleanup.summary: TASK-013 created no temporary artifact inside the checkout: every command that imports a checkout module ran with -B, Cargo built into /mnt/F/Nexees-toolchains/target/, the Desktop window was built in its desktop/ folder there and installed for testing in desktop-install/, and the negative-test copies, the step-logging copy of the end-to-end test and the evidence scripts used the session scratch folder. The private profiles of the end-to-end runs lived in the system temporary folder and each run removed its own, except one run that its time limit cut off: its kept host was stopped by its process ID once its program was seen to be the disposable installation's host, and its profile folder was then removed. The two placeholders the task implemented were removed with rm. At the close, scripts/test/task_cleanup.py ran on the checkout with an empty TASK-013 manifest, first as a plan and then with --apply and its record: it removed nothing, refused nothing, and left in place 17 untracked files, the new source files and the TASK-013 evidence, each with its hash. The ignored files are the owner's IDE output (rust-analyzer's target/ and the Java extension's .gradle/ beside TASK-003's prototype) and the editor's link apps/desktop/node_modules, none task-owned, all left exactly as they are. The disposable installation and the scratch files of this task are removed once this receipt is committed and pushed; the Desktop build folder stays beside the Cargo target folder as a build cache, and the copy of the evidence scripts in /mnt/F/Nexees-toolchains/task-tools/ stays for the rest of this run of tasks. No pre-existing or user-owned file was deleted, reset or stashed, and no command of the task wrote in the owner's toolchain and cache folders: every tool of the task refuses to run without the isolated toolchain.

manual_impact.detail: docs/manuals/NEXEES_USER_MANUAL.md section 3 now says how the Desktop's workspaces work: the folder a window shows is its workspace, and a folder opened becomes a Code workspace named after it the first time; Nexees: New Workspace… makes a Code or LCL workspace of a folder with a name, Nexees: Open Workspace… lists the workspaces and shows the one chosen, and Nexees: Close Workspace leaves the window without a folder; a folder belongs to one workspace only, and Nexees says which workspace it would overlap; a workspace whose folder was moved or replaced by a link is not opened; a workspace keeps its identity across restarts; and every window still counts as one view. The end-to-end test checks on the installed application what the window does of these; the registry's and the host's tests check the moved or replaced folder and the restart. The LCL manual is unchanged (TASK-013_EVIDENCE.md section 9).
